summary.en: London’s blues revival raised a generation of blues fans who later led rock bands.
summary.zh: 伦敦的布鲁斯复兴运动孕育了一批布鲁斯爱好者，他们后来成为了摇滚乐队的领军者。

body.zh:
之前有提到，伦敦在60年代初期掀起了一场浩大的布鲁斯复兴（Blues Revival）运动，很多音乐团体都参与其中。这里我不想讨论那些单曲上榜的乐队，而是发生在地下布鲁斯发烧友之间的事。

我们提及伦敦发生的事时，必须铭记一点，这些人模仿的很多布鲁斯唱片并不容易得到。独立厂牌在美国出售这些唱片，而厂牌在本国就有一些分销问题，更别提把唱片引进到英国了。因此很多时候，你必须通过邮购得到布鲁斯音乐的唱片，当你几个礼拜后拿到唱片，拆开它们，也许你就是镇上唯一或是极少之一拥有这张唱片的人，人们会聚在一起给别人听听自己的唱片，有点像唱片音乐派对。因为每个人收藏的唱片都不同，没有收音机的情况下，这很实用，可以让你听到你自己没买的音乐。

到了晚上，音乐家们将忠实地再现这些音乐， 大多数是芝加哥布鲁斯（Chicago Blues）。一些非常重要的音乐人将会参与到日后布鲁斯派的英伦入侵中，值得一提的是The Rolling Stones (滚石)。他们参与了早期的布鲁斯乐队，由Alexis Korner和Cyril Davies领衔，称为Blues Incorporated，他们在Marquee剧院创立了布鲁斯之夜，就在伦敦郊外的伊灵。

这些布鲁斯之夜通常在闲暇的夜晚，周日晚上或周三晚上，俱乐部里可能一个人都没有，于是俱乐部老板让你的布鲁斯乐团进驻表演，这些表演不在重要的周五或周六晚上进行。这些表演强烈再现了Chess Records的芝加哥电声布鲁斯（Chicago Electric Blues），重现了人声、和声、吉他、鼓和钢琴等等。

当你听到现存的由Alexis Korner和Cyril Davies这些人录制的唱片时，如果你不知道他是个穿花呢外套叼着烟斗的英国中产阶级，你肯定以为他来自50年代末的一个芝加哥俱乐部，他们非常致敬那个时代的布鲁斯。你会目睹很多20多、30多、40多岁的人来表演致敬，也会有年轻人出现，比如Keith Richards和Mick Jagger（The Rolling Stones成员），坐在前排观看这些人在干什么。事实上Mick Jagger的第一次演唱机会就是顶替别人的，被顶替的那个人叫Long John Baldry，本应他在Blues Incorporated演唱的当晚，得到了去BBC的机会，于是Mick Jagger代替了他。由于长期看表演，Mick对曲调很熟悉。这个布鲁斯狂热者的小舞台，很像伦敦的布鲁斯俱乐部，处在该环境下的很多年轻音乐家，随后都成为了The Rolling Stones、Yardbirds这些乐队中的一员，他们就是在这样的环境中熟悉布鲁斯音乐的。

这与The Beatles的经历大不相同，Beatles也接触了很多来自美国的音乐，但这是由于利物浦是个港口城市，如我之前所说，水手们经过美国时会购买大量唱片，因为他们知道这能卖个好价钱，就像人们今天在eBays上做的一样。他们途经美国，买很多唱片，带回利物浦，卖给人们，因此相对于伦敦的布鲁斯发烧友，Beatles可以接触到更多的美国音乐。但Beatles对布鲁斯不太感兴趣，如果你认真搜寻他们作品中突出的布鲁斯音乐，不会有多大发现，他们更感兴趣的是优美的声乐歌曲。但The Rolling Stones和布鲁斯俱乐部中的其他人，真正热爱的是芝加哥电声布鲁斯。下节课我们就来讨论一下The Rolling Stones以及他们是如何在英美崭露头角的。
body.en:
As mentioned earlier, early-1960s London saw a large blues revival; many groups took part. I do not want to talk about chart singles here, but about what happened among underground blues enthusiasts.

When we talk about London we must remember: many of the blues records these people imitated were hard to get. Independents sold them in the U.S., and even at home distribution was shaky—let alone importing to Britain. So often you ordered by mail; weeks later you opened the package and maybe you were the only person in town—or one of very few—with that record. People gathered to play each other their records, a bit like record parties. Because collections differed, and without radio, it was practical—you heard music you had not bought yourself.

At night musicians faithfully recreated the music—mostly Chicago blues. Some very important players would later join the blues wing of the British Invasion; worth naming are the Rolling Stones. They took part in early blues bands led by Alexis Korner and Cyril Davies—Blues Incorporated—who started blues nights at the Marquee, out in Ealing near London.

Those blues nights usually fell on quiet evenings—Sunday or Wednesday—when the club might be empty, so the owner let a blues band in; not on key Friday or Saturday nights. The shows strongly recreated Chess Records Chicago electric blues: voice, harmony, guitar, drums, piano, and so on.

If you hear surviving records by people like Alexis Korner and Cyril Davies, and you did not know he was a tweed-jacket, pipe-smoking British middle-class man, you would swear he came from a late-1950s Chicago club—they paid deep homage to that blues. You would see people in their twenties, thirties, forties playing tribute, and young people too—Keith Richards and Mick Jagger (Rolling Stones)—sitting up front watching. In fact Mick’s first singing chance was filling in for someone else: Long John Baldry was due to sing with Blues Incorporated that night but got a BBC date, so Mick took his place. Having watched so long, Mick knew the tunes. This little stage of blues fanatics was much like London’s blues clubs; many young musicians in that world later joined the Rolling Stones, Yardbirds, and so on—they learned blues in that setting.

That differs sharply from the Beatles’ path. The Beatles also heard a lot of American music, but because Liverpool is a port: as I said, sailors passing through America bought stacks of records knowing they would sell well back home—like eBay today. They bought in the U.S., brought them to Liverpool, sold them; so relative to London blues fans, the Beatles could access more American music. But the Beatles were not very interested in blues; if you hunt hard for prominent blues in their work you will not find much—they cared more about fine vocal songs. The Rolling Stones and others in the blues clubs truly loved Chicago electric blues. Next lecture: the Rolling Stones and how they broke through in Britain and America.
